t: Rings and Rods — One Bitmask Per Rod
o: **Understanding the problem.** The input is a flat string of color/rod pairs, and we must count rods carrying at least one ring of every color. For `B0B6G0R6R0R6G9`: rod 0 collects B, G, R (all three), rod 6 only B and R, rod 9 only G — answer 1. Example 2 piles six rings of all colors onto rod 0 alone (still answer 1), and one lone ring like `G4` can never complete a rod (answer 0). Duplicates are irrelevant: what matters per rod is only WHICH colors appeared, never how many rings. With at most 100 pairs efficiency is moot — clarity and clean bookkeeping win.
k: Per rod only the SET of colors present matters — a 3-bit mask (R=1, G=2, B=4) captures it.
"Has all three colors" reduces to mask == 7.
Colors sit at even indices and rods at odd ones, so parsing is a stride-2 loop.
Duplicate pairs are harmless: OR-ing an already-set bit is a no-op.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Map of Color Sets
a.i: Map each rod label to the set of colors seen on it, then count sets of size three. The most direct transcription of the statement, and it generalizes instantly to more colors or unbounded rod labels.
s: Walk pairs: color = rings[i], rod = rings[i+1].
Add the color to the set keyed by that rod.
Count entries whose set has size 3.
a.sp: O(1) — bounded by 10 rods x 3 colors regardless of input size.

a.i: Ten integers replace the map entirely: OR bit 1/2/4 into mask[rod] for every pair, then count masks equal to 7. No hashing or sets — typically the shortest, fastest solution, and a nice showcase of bitmask presence tracking.
s: Translate the color char to a bit: R -> 1, G -> 2, B -> 4.
Return the number of masks equal to 7.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over the pairs.

w: Either version lands in minutes; name the pattern explicitly — bitmasks track presence of up-to-32 flags and make membership checks one instruction. Pitfalls: reading the pair order backwards (color comes FIRST, rod second); counting rods with any ring instead of all three; forgetting rod digits are characters in typed languages (`rings[i+1] - '0'`). Follow-ups: report which rods qualify, or generalize to more colors — masks scale to 64 bits, sets scale further.
